description: I'm Miles, like Usogui and programming. Also like NASA.
summary: The project helps users with varying levels of expertise understand how fire behaves on Earth and in microgravity. It addresses the challenge by using Super Intelligence (SI) to summarize data on fire safety, guiding users and ranking evidence for selected mission atmospheres, flagging materials that may soften or warp near published temperature limits. It additionally has a tool to analyze CAD materials, giving a report about the temperature limits of the materials. If a user is ever stuck or requires help, a chatbot is available to speak to. It is important because it increases the velocity at which you can research materials, fuels, and other subjects related to microgravity missions. Its capabilities are expressly focused on ensuring that users have an easier way of accessing data about their own CAD projects, and their own research.
details: The project helps users with varying levels of expertise understand how fire behaves on Earth and in microgravity. The site aims to easily and effectively showcase combustion conditions in microgravity and in normal conditions, bridging data from NASA and other sources to highlight safety risks that materials may present, and use SI to rank evidence for specific atmospheres. Additionally, the website is intended to function as a tool for CAD users; with the implementation of a material checker for CAD, that flags materials that could potentially break or warp if exposed to high-temperature conditions. In this project, I used TypeScript primarily, with CSS and JavaScript also in the project. I did not use any hardware, however I used the free domain given to participants, connected it to Vercel, and deployed the website with Node.js. For helping tools, when I was unavailable to be at my computer, I utilized Cursor's cloud agent and Codex to accelerate development when a computer was not available. Additionally I utilized a Gemini API to generate real-time SI responses and a Upstash URL to limit request volume. Both combined gives users the ability to query and search on the website even easier. For the last API, I used a render API to call LibreDWG, and convert DWG files to DXF, and check them against the list of possible materials. The project is creative as a user could come in and read about fire in orbit, asking the HelpBot for clarification along the way, or they could be developing a CAD project, and are researching materials, using the HelpBot for finding research. It's a multi-dimensional project that is intended to be useful for professionals and the general public as well. For the website, I first considered functionality, and what I wanted the project to serve as. Initially, I just took the prompt at face value, planning to implement a website to serve data to the user better than just looking up many different research articles, however I realized I wanted the website to do more than that. When I thought of effects of heat on space missions, I think of what it does to the parts of the craft, and how well they can withstand different temperatures. So, I decided to aim to help the people who design those parts in the starting stage: CAD. It's unrealistic to try to build an engine that can analyze the actual physics of CAD designs in two days, however I could build something to analyze their parts, and give feedback to the user. For the last factor, I considered how the website itself looked. If it was incredibly hard to read and difficult to navigate, users wouldn't want to stay on the page, and the more professional it looks the better the users will feel of their experiences as well. So I separated research categories, and made the website feel good to navigate, natural and intuitive, but not spelling everything out for the user.
